problem: Standard instruction-following navigation metrics (SR, SPL, NE, OSR) look only at the final node. Path-aware alternatives are also flawed: SED requires exact action matches and harshly penalizes near-misses in (quasi-)continuous spaces, while CLS ignores node order. AD and MD ignore order too. None of them properly measures an agent's fidelity to the reference trajectory.
motivation: Instructions describe paths, not just goals: 'pick up the newspaper at the front door, leave it in my bedroom and come back' fails if the agent visits the right places in the wrong order, yet CLS scores the reversed path the same. The field needs one metric that is order-sensitive, softly penalizes deviations, is invariant to the scale and density of nodes, works in both graph-based and continuous settings, and is cheap enough to serve as an RL reward. Dynamic Time Warping, long used for aligning time series in speech and gesture recognition, has these properties.
key_idea: Score path fidelity with Dynamic Time Warping between the reference and agent paths, using shortest-path distance as the element cost. The cost is normalized by |R|·d_th and passed through exp(-x) to give nDTW in [0,1], and nDTW multiplied by success gives SDTW.
insight: DTW's monotone alignment forces the endpoints to match and preserves order, so it captures both the goal and the route while penalizing deviations softly rather than all-or-nothing. In a human ranking study (2525 samples, 9 raters), sign tests show nDTW correlates better with human preferences than every unconstrained metric: vs CLS 162/46 (p=2.4e-16), vs NE 254/9. SDTW likewise beats all success-constrained metrics, e.g. vs SPL 219/17 and vs SED 213/26. The R4R experiments expose other metrics' blind spots. SED scores random paths (16.5) higher than trained agents (9.6/9.4). SR and SED do not separate goal-oriented from fidelity-oriented agents. SPL's gap (15.0 vs 21.4) reflects matching path length, not fidelity. SDTW gives the clearest joint success-plus-fidelity signal, and using nDTW as the RL reward improves nearly all metrics.
method: DTW for navigation: optimal monotone alignment W between the reference path R and query path Q, with step sizes (1,1),(1,0),(0,1) and boundary conditions w1=(1,1), w_end=(|R|,|Q|); the element cost is shortest-path graph distance (Dijkstra), Euclidean distance, or precomputed grid-point distances in continuous environments with obstacles.

nDTW normalization: nDTW = exp(-DTW(R,Q)/(|R|·d_th)). Dividing by |R|·d_th removes sensitivity to scale and node density, and the negative exponential bounds the score in [0,1] with higher meaning better.
SDTW: SDTW = SR·nDTW, a single summary metric that is nonzero only for successful episodes (within d_th of the goal) and is weighted by path fidelity.

Computation: exact O(|R||Q|) dynamic programming over the cumulative cost matrix C (C[i][j] = δ + min of three predecessors, C00=0, borders=inf); approximate linear time and space via FastDTW, adapted to discrete graphs by sampling nodes.

Human evaluation protocol: random 15×15 jittered-grid graphs (ζ=0.3, edges if distance ≤1.4, d_th = 1.33 × mean edge length). Raters rank 5 query paths per fixed reference path. Metrics are compared per set by rank correlation with humans, and a sign/binomial test is run over sets, in an unconstrained (UC) and a success-constrained (SC) study.

nDTW as RL reward: the fidelity-oriented agent's per-step reward is nDTW(q1..i+1,R) − nDTW(q1..i,R), with terminal reward 1 − d(q_f,g)/d_th only on success (d_th=3m). The goal-oriented comparison agent is rewarded for distance reduction plus ±1 for success or failure.

numbers_note: Only one navigation results table (Table 2), on R2R and R4R val-unseen. The random baseline is excluded here: R2R SR 5.1 / nDTW 27.9 / SDTW 3.6; R4R SR 13.7 / nDTW 18.5 / SDTW 4.1. The human-judgment study results are sign-test counts and p-values (Table 1), not navigation metrics. There is no comparison to published state-of-the-art agents.
results: In the human study, nDTW beats every unconstrained metric (e.g. 162/46 vs CLS, p=2.4e-16; 254/9 vs NE) and SDTW beats every success-constrained metric (e.g. 219/17 vs SPL, 213/26 vs SED) in correlation with human path rankings. Replacing the goal-oriented reward with the nDTW reward improves R2R val-unseen SPL from 38.4 to 41.4, CLS from 53.5 to 57.5, nDTW from 54.4 to 58.3 and SDTW from 36.1 to 38.3. On R4R val-unseen it raises SPL from 15.0 to 21.4, nDTW from 26.9 to 30.4 and SDTW from 11.4 to 12.6, while SR and SED stay essentially flat (28.7 → 28.5 and 9.6 → 9.4).
limitations: The human-judgment study uses synthetic random 2D jittered-grid graphs and paths, not real indoor or outdoor environments or instructions.

The RL demonstration is small: one agent architecture in the authors' own implementation, compared only with a goal-oriented reward and a random baseline, with no comparison to published state-of-the-art agents. SR and SED do not improve on R4R.
The nDTW scale depends on the choice of d_th. Continuous environments with obstacles need precomputed grid distances, so scores are approximate there.
